summary: This document specifies how UDPTL, the main transport used for T.38 fax, can be carried over DTLS. It also covers how this is indicated in SDP and negotiated in sessions set up with SIP.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7345 shows how to carry T.38 fax over the Internet with encryption and tamper detection. It adds a DTLS layer between the fax transport and UDP, so fax data is protected without changing the fax protocol itself. It also defines how the two ends of a call agree to use it, using SDP attributes inside a SIP session.

questions: how does t.38 fax work over dtls
subtitle: How T.38 fax packets are carried inside DTLS, and how SDP signals that both ends agree to do it.

tldr.problem: Fax sent over IP with UDPTL travels unprotected, even though fax often carries sensitive personal, corporate and governmental data. The earlier fax security options saw little market adoption.
tldr.mechanism: A DTLS layer is placed between UDPTL and UDP, and the two endpoints agree to it through SDP using a new UDP/TLS/UDPTL proto value, a setup attribute for the DTLS roles and a fingerprint attribute for the certificate.
tldr.outcome: Fax gets integrity and confidentiality protection without changing UDPTL or the layers above it. RFC 7345 has since been updated by RFC 8842.

today: RFC 7345 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 8842. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Fax Needed a New Approach
sections.content:
Fax over the traditional telephone network was rarely protected. The reasoning was that intercepting a fax required physical access to the telephone equipment, so the cost of adding security was rarely justified.

Real-time communication is moving to IP networks, where a message can be intercepted or its sender impersonated. The RFC states that a level of protection giving both integrity and confidentiality is now vital for fax.

The overwhelmingly predominant fax transport protocol is UDPTL, as described in Section 9.1 of the ITU-T T.38 recommendation. Two earlier ways of securing fax existed. Annex H of the ITU-T T.30 recommendation specifies application-layer protection for Group 3 fax equipment based on RSA, independent of the transport. The ITU-T T.38 recommendation also specifies fax transport over RTP with SRTP, which protects fax in IP networks.

Both options had been available for years and neither gained meaningful adoption. A study by the 3rd Generation Partnership Project on secure fax in the IP Multimedia Subsystem found that the best result came from carrying UDPTL over DTLS, which is what this RFC specifies.
sections.plainLanguage: Fax on the telephone network was rarely encrypted, because intercepting it meant getting physical access to the phone line. Over IP networks, a fax can be read or forged by anyone on the path, so protection matters. Two earlier security options existed for IP fax, but neither was widely used.

sections.title: The Protocol Stack
sections.content:
The stack for fax over UDPTL normally runs the Internet facsimile protocol on top of UDPTL, on top of UDP, on top of IP. This RFC inserts a DTLS layer between UDPTL and UDP. The facsimile protocol and the UDPTL layer above it are unchanged.

The RFC lists the reasons for this choice. The DTLS design is well defined and understood, and implementations are widely available. No extensions to DTLS are needed to carry UDPTL over it. Only the insertion of the DTLS layer is required, so the layers above UDPTL need no modification. UDPTL is by far the most widely deployed fax transport protocol in IP networks. And 3GPP and the IP fax community need a way to carry UDPTL over DTLS to provide secure fax in SIP-based networks, including the IP Multimedia Subsystem.

The transport uses the DTLS record layer application_data packets. A DTLS record does not say whether it carries UDPTL or something else, so the use of a dedicated DTLS association for UDPTL has to be negotiated. The RFC does that with the Session Description Protocol and its offer and answer mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: The change to the stack is small: a DTLS layer goes between UDPTL and UDP. Nothing above UDPTL changes, and DTLS needs no new features for this. The DTLS records do not name the protocol they carry, so the two ends must agree in advance to use that DTLS association for fax.

sections.title: The Secure Channel
sections.content:
The media stream is negotiated with the SDP offer and answer mechanism. DTLS itself is used exactly as specified in RFC 6347.

Once the DTLS handshake has completed successfully, the UDPTL packets MUST be transported in DTLS record layer application_data packets. The RFC states the reason for that ordering: the handshake is completed first so that facsimile data cannot be transmitted insecurely.

The RFC also fixes its own terms. DTLS uses the word session for a long-lived set of keying material that spans several DTLS associations. This RFC uses session for a multimedia session, DTLS session for the DTLS construct, and DTLS association for one cipher suite and keying material set bound to a single host and port quartet. The same DTLS session can establish the keying material for several associations.
sections.plainLanguage: The fax packets travel inside DTLS records, and only after the DTLS handshake has finished. That order matters, because it keeps the fax data from being sent unprotected. In this RFC a DTLS association is one set of keys and one cipher suite for one address and port pair.

sections.title: The SDP Attributes for the Stream
sections.content:
Each endpoint must create an SDP media description, the m= line, for every UDPTL-over-DTLS media stream, and must set the proto field of that line to UDP/TLS/UDPTL. The RFC registers that value in the SDP proto field registry.

Two groups of SDP attributes are used: the attributes defined for UDPTL over UDP in the ITU-T T.38 recommendation, and the attributes from RFC 4145 and RFC 4572 that this RFC describes. The endpoint must not use the SDP connection attribute, and must use the setup attribute to negotiate the DTLS roles.

If the endpoint supports a cipher suite with an associated certificate, it must include a fingerprint attribute. It must support SHA-256 for producing and checking the fingerprint value, and SHA-256 is preferred. UDPTL over DTLS must support TLS_DHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 and must support TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, and it must prefer the ECDHE suite and any other Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS) cipher suites over the ones without it. Implementations should disable TLS-level compression.

If the handshake selects a cipher suite with a certificate, the certificate received in the handshake must match the fingerprint received in the SDP attribute. If it does not match, the endpoint must tear the media session down immediately. An endpoint may wait for the other side's fingerprint before it establishes the connection, but that may add delay.
sections.plainLanguage: Both ends describe the fax stream in SDP. The media line names the protocol UDP/TLS/UDPTL, a setup attribute says who sends the DTLS hello message, and a fingerprint attribute carries a hash of the sender's certificate. The receiving end hashes the certificate it gets in the handshake and compares it with the fingerprint. If they differ, it drops the call at once.

sections.title: Choosing the DTLS Roles
sections.content:
The offerer should set the setup attribute to actpass, unless it insists on one role. In that case it may use active, meaning it will send the DTLS ClientHello, or passive, meaning it will receive it. The offerer must not use holdconn. If the offerer used actpass or passive, it must be ready to receive a DTLS ClientHello before the SDP answer arrives.

If the answerer accepts the stream, it must set setup to active or passive, and must not use holdconn. When it chooses active, it must start the DTLS handshake by sending a ClientHello on the negotiated media stream to the offerer's address and port. If the offerer ends up active after reading the answer, it must send the ClientHello to the answerer's address and port.

After the offer and answer exchange, either endpoint may send a new offer to modify the session. If the fingerprint values and transport parameters are unchanged, the endpoints can reuse the existing DTLS association. Otherwise they negotiate and create a new association and then delete the old one, and each endpoint must be ready to receive data on both associations while both are alive.
sections.plainLanguage: The setup attribute decides which end sends the first DTLS message. The offerer usually leaves the choice open, and the answerer then picks a side. The side that picks active sends the DTLS hello message and starts the handshake. When a session changes, the two ends can keep the same DTLS association or build a new one.

sections.title: NAT Traversal, Rekeying and Falling Back
sections.content:
When Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) is used, the ICE checks run before the DTLS handshake starts. In aggressive nomination mode several candidate pairs may be marked valid before ICE settles on one, so user agents must treat all candidate pairs of a single component as part of the same DTLS association. There is then only one DTLS handshake, and the endpoint may need to adjust its IP addresses if the chosen pair shifts. After an ICE restart the handshake is repeated and a new association is created, and the previous association is deleted once the new one exists.

STUN packets must be sent directly over UDP, not over DTLS. To sort out what arrives on the address and port of the DTLS association, the first byte of the packet decides: a value of 0 or 1 means the packet is STUN, and a value between 20 and 63 inclusive means it is DTLS.

During rekeying, packets protected by the old keys can arrive after the new handshake has completed, because packets can be reordered on the wire. Receivers must therefore keep both sets of keys for a while, so that older packets can still be decrypted and verified. How long the old keys are kept is out of scope.

If the other end does not support UDPTL over DTLS, a secure fax stream cannot be set up. A caller who is willing to fall back to plain UDPTL over UDP can offer both, using the SDP capability negotiation mechanism of RFC 5939, or send a new offer for a UDPTL-over-UDP stream after the secure offer is rejected.
sections.plainLanguage: Three practical issues come with running fax over DTLS. ICE checks run before the handshake, and STUN traffic stays in plain UDP so that the receiver can tell STUN and DTLS packets apart by their first byte. After a rekey, the receiver keeps the old keys for a while because reordered packets may still arrive under them. And a secure fax call needs both ends to support it, so the caller can offer a plain UDPTL stream as well.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Fax can carry personal, corporate and governmental information, so protecting the confidentiality and integrity of the data is critical. This document provides both by specifying fax transport over DTLS.

A DTLS media stream negotiated with SIP and SDP needs a way to confirm that the certificate received over DTLS was issued by the other party of the SIP session. The usual DTLS method gives the server, and optionally the client, a PKIX certificate that the client checks against the server's domain name. That works because there are few servers, and issuing certificates to all clients is not realistic in most deployments.

The design therefore leans on the integrity of the SIP signalling instead of on confidentiality of it. As long as each side can verify the integrity of the SDP it receives, the DTLS handshake cannot be hijacked with a man-in-the-middle attack. The caller can provide that integrity to the callee with the SIP Identity mechanism, and S/MIME or other mechanisms could serve the same purpose.

Without such an integrity mechanism the mechanism still works, but the security is limited to protection against passive attacks by intermediaries. An active attack on the signalling combined with an active attack on the media plane can let an attacker attack the connection, which is the R-SIG-MEDIA case in the notation of RFC 5479.
sections.plainLanguage: The DTLS channel protects the fax data itself. What it does not do is prove that the peer is who the SIP session says it is. That proof comes from the integrity of the SDP message, for example through SIP Identity. Without it, an attacker could still tamper with the signalling and with the media at the same time.

sections.title: An Example Call Flow
sections.content:
The appendix gives a full example. Both ends generate self-signed certificates, used for a single session or reused across sessions. The SIP signalling travels over TLS so that the caller has an integrity-protected channel with its identity service, and the identity service asserts the caller's identity and protects the SIP message. Transport between proxies should also be protected.

Alice acts as the passive endpoint of the DTLS association and Bob as the active one. The flow runs: a SIP INVITE from Alice to her proxy carrying the SDP offer, the same INVITE forwarded by the proxy to Bob, a DTLS ClientHello from Bob directly to Alice, the remaining DTLS handshake messages, a SIP 200 OK from Bob to the proxy and from the proxy to Alice, a SIP ACK from Alice, and then the T.38 fax messages carried over UDPTL inside DTLS.

The SDP offer in the example carries the media line m=image 6056 UDP/TLS/UDPTL t38, a setup attribute with the value actpass, and a fingerprint attribute holding the hash of Alice's self-signed certificate.
sections.plainLanguage: The example call shows the order of the messages. The caller sends a SIP invite that carries the SDP offer, the proxy forwards it, and the far end answers with the SIP 200 OK. In between, the DTLS handshake runs directly between the two endpoints, and the fax messages follow inside DTLS.

viz.caption: What the design protects, and what it does not

items.title: Fax data
items.text: DTLS gives the fax data integrity and confidentiality.

items.title: Certificate check
items.text: The certificate from the handshake must match the SDP fingerprint, or the session is torn down.

items.title: Peer identity
items.text: Proving the peer is the SIP session partner comes from the integrity of the SDP, not from DTLS.

items.title: Without that proof
items.text: Only passive attacks by intermediaries are stopped, which is the R-SIG-MEDIA case.
